# SpotIt: Evaluating Text-to-SQL Evaluation with Formal Verification

[All reading notes](../reading-notes.md) · [Catalog entry](../README.md#spotit)

**Full paper read · 2026-11-09**

[Original source](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.26840v2) · arXiv:2510.26840v2, 4 March 2026; PDF identifies publication at ICLR 2026

**Reading coverage:** All 37 pages: main sections 1–7, references, Appendices A–G, runtime tables, all counterexample examples, semantic encodings and full proof derivations. Main result charts and DISTINCT example visually inspected.

## Research question

Two SQL queries can agree on a benchmark database while differing on another valid instance; conversely, a gold query may itself be wrong or represent only one plausible interpretation.

## Method

SpotIt extends VeriEQL with string/date operations and type conversions, searches successively larger bounded symbolic databases, validates generated counterexamples in the backend and optionally cross-checks counterexamples across systems.

## Evaluation

Ten systems are re-evaluated on 1,533 BIRD development questions, searching primarily execution-passing pairs up to five rows per relation with 600-second verifier limits. Additional tests cover 135 SQLite Spider 2.0 questions and a manual sample of 50 CSC-32B discrepancies.

## What the results support

The verifier supports roughly 94–97% of BIRD execution-passing pairs and finds additional differences that change rankings. In the 50-case audit, 64% are attributed to problematic gold SQL, 26% to predictions and 10% to ambiguity; these are discrepancy-sample proportions.

## Limits and qualifications

Counterexamples establish query disagreement, not which interpretation satisfies the user. No-counterexample results may reflect bounds, unsupported syntax or timeout. Runtime averages below four seconds cover successful counterexample cases. Window functions, recursive queries and ordering nondeterminism remain limitations; some appendix examples have semantic inconsistencies requiring care before reuse.

## Relevance to reliable Text-to-SQL

Strong evidence for separating reference equivalence from natural-language correctness, and for inspecting small counterexamples when auditing benchmark labels or accepting generated SQL.
